title: About
text:
Sebastian Jaramillo
I am a Ph.D. candidate in Mathematics at the University of Oregon. My research lies at the intersection of probability, Markov chain Monte Carlo methods, and the mathematical analysis of sampling algorithms.
Alongside my doctoral research, I have developed a strong applied interest in time series, econometrics, causal inference, machine learning, and quantitative finance. I am currently building a technical portfolio that translates my mathematical training into applied projects relevant for industry roles.
My long-term goal is to work on quantitative problems where rigorous mathematical thinking, statistical modeling, and computational implementation meet.

title: Projects
text:
Featured Portfolio

Time Series and Bayesian Econometrics
A sequence of studies in Bayesian learning, policy-response inference, recession probabilities, and dynamic shock transmission. The first project has an existing analysis notebook; Projects 02 and 03 provide executable Python packages, scientific controls, notebooks, and research reports. Later projects remain research designs.
Browse the repository or examine the completed work below.

Bayesian learning and posterior prediction
Project 01. How do prior beliefs and observations change posterior predictions for discrete outcomes? The existing notebook develops binary and count models, prior sensitivity, and posterior prediction, including the supplied PGA scoring data. This is existing notebook-based work; it has not been converted into the package architecture used by the later studies.
Project overview · Analysis notebook


Monetary policy and recession risk
Project 02. Do policy responses to economic slack require separate slopes, and what do financial indicators reveal about recession risk twelve months ahead?
The policy analysis uses 239 U.S. quarters, 1955Q1–2014Q3. The symmetric rule receives 96.4% posterior model probability within the two specified alternatives under the primary prior. The long-run inflation response has posterior median 1.60 and a central 90% interval of [0.95, 2.48]. Residual dependence limits the policy interpretation.
The recession application makes forecast origins, target dates, and label availability explicit. In its twelve observed 2008 targets, Brier loss improves relative to a matched frequency benchmark while negative log score worsens. This revised-data, pseudo-real-time exercise does not establish general forecasting superiority.
The Python implementation separates data contracts, priors, models, Gibbs samplers, posterior results, and forecast evaluation. Independent numerical integration checks model evidence; scientific controls run in continuous integration.
Research report (PDF) · Executive summary · Executed notebook · Code and reproduction


Persistence and shock propagation
Project 03. How can models with the same long-run shock total produce different transmission paths, and how does persistence change the precision of an average?
Three stable autoregressive specifications share an infinite accumulated response of ten to a one-unit innovation, but their responses differ in timing and variance. One stable AR(2) initially amplifies the innovation by 20% before decaying. Root analysis separates stable, unstable, and unit-circle cases; a finite moving-average control distinguishes stationarity from invertibility.
In the designed stationary AR(1), 200 observations have the mean-estimation precision of 11.05 independent observations. Across 10,000 replications, a nominal 95% interval that assumes independence attains only 35.27% coverage. These are controlled known-parameter simulation results, not estimates from an observed economic dataset or posterior credible intervals.
Responses are checked through companion matrices, recursion, controlled shock paths, and an independent linear filter. The object-oriented package records seeds, initial conditions, burn-in, numerical errors, and artifact checksums.
Research report (PDF) · Executive summary · Executed notebook · Code and reproduction


Research designs in progress
The remaining designs address lag uncertainty and Bayesian model averaging (04), GDP distributions and growth at risk (05), payroll forecasts with macroeconomic information (06), employment forecasts through extreme episodes (07), and common factors and structural interpretation (08). Their implementations and reproduced results are pending; see the project catalog for scope and status.

section: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and Sampling Algorithms
text:
Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and Sampling Algorithms
My current research studies Hamiltonian Monte Carlo-type algorithms, coupling methods, and convergence behavior for probability distributions with geometric structure.
I am particularly interested in how algorithmic design choices affect mixing, stability, contraction, and convergence rates.
When correlated draws help. Can correlated samples give a more precise estimate? Use a circle to see how the answer changes with the quantity being averaged, then reproduce a simulation of the exact sampler in my dissertation.

My applied portfolio connects Bayesian inference with economic questions and reproducible computation. Recent studies examine monetary policy and recession risk and persistence and shock propagation, with research reports, executed notebooks, and numerical controls.

title: Research
text:
Applied econometrics and time-series dynamics
The time-series portfolio develops a practical connection between sampling theory and applied econometrics. Bayesian policy-rule comparison and recession probabilities use explicit priors, posterior simulation, and forecast information sets. Controlled autoregressive experiments examine stability, shock transmission, and the precision of time averages.
Each analysis separates numerical verification from economic interpretation. The policy study documents residual and data-vintage limitations; the dynamics study identifies its findings as known-parameter simulation results.
